solution:
**Statement.** Avogadro's law (§1.5) states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules. It was proposed by Avogadro in 1811.

**Explanation.** Consider the formation of water vapour from hydrogen and oxygen at the same temperature and pressure:

\(\text{Hydrogen (g)} + \text{Oxygen (g)} \longrightarrow \text{Water (g)}\)

100 mL + 50 mL \(\longrightarrow\) 100 mL, that is 2 volumes : 1 volume : 2 volumes (Gay Lussac's law).

If one volume contains \(n\) molecules, then by Avogadro's law the two volumes of hydrogen contain \(2n\) molecules, the one volume of oxygen contains \(n\) molecules, and the two volumes of water vapour contain \(2n\) molecules. So

\(2n\) molecules of hydrogen + \(n\) molecules of oxygen \(\longrightarrow\) \(2n\) molecules of water,

which reduces to 2 molecules of hydrogen combining with 1 molecule of oxygen to give 2 molecules of water vapour, with no oxygen left over.

This is the law's real value: it converts a ratio of measured VOLUMES into a ratio of NUMBERS of molecules. It also forced the distinction between an atom and a molecule — the result above only makes sense if hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic, as the chapter notes, so Avogadro had to treat the gas particles as polyatomic molecules rather than single atoms.

The two quantities describe the same element on completely different scales — one is the mass of a single atom, the other the mass of a mole of atoms.

**12 u of carbon** is a mass expressed in unified mass units. An atom of carbon-12 is assigned a mass of exactly 12.00000 u by definition (§1.7.1), so 12 u of carbon is the mass of just ONE carbon-12 atom. In grams that is \(12 \times 1.66056 \times 10^{-24} = 1.99 \times 10^{-23}\) g.

**12 g of carbon** is the molar mass of carbon (§1.8), because the molar mass in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass in u. It is therefore the mass of ONE MOLE of carbon atoms, that is \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

So the difference is a factor of Avogadro's constant: 12 g of carbon contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) times as many atoms as 12 u of carbon does. The chapter derives exactly this by dividing the molar mass by the measured mass of one atom:

\(\dfrac{12\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{1.992648 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{g\ atom^{-1}}} = 6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}\)

The chapter fixes the conversion between the two mass scales as \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\) (§1.7.1), and Problem 1.1 gives the mass of an atom of hydrogen as \(1.0080\ \mathrm{u}\).

Mass of one hydrogen atom

\(= 1.0080\ \mathrm{u} \times 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g\ u^{-1}}\)

\(= 1.674 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\)

If the rounded-off atomic mass of \(1.0\ \mathrm{u}\) from the chapter's table is used instead, the answer is \(1.66 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\); the two agree to the precision the data allow.

The same result follows from the molar mass, which is a useful cross-check: \(\dfrac{1.008\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.674 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g\ atom^{-1}}\).

Molecular mass is the sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms in the molecule (§1.7.3). Using the chapter's rounded-off average atomic masses H = 1.0 u, C = 12.0 u, N = 14.0 u, O = 16.0 u:

**a. \(\mathrm{NH_3}\)**

\(= 14.0 + 3 \times 1.0 = 17.0\ \mathrm{u}\)

**b. \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)** (2 C, 4 H, 2 O)

\(= 2 \times 12.0 + 4 \times 1.0 + 2 \times 16.0 = 24.0 + 4.0 + 32.0 = 60.0\ \mathrm{u}\)

**c. \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)** (2 C, 6 H, 1 O)

\(= 2 \times 12.0 + 6 \times 1.0 + 16.0 = 24.0 + 6.0 + 16.0 = 46.0\ \mathrm{u}\)

Count the hydrogens carefully in the last two: acetic acid has 4 (three on the methyl group, one on the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\)) and ethanol has 6 (five on the ethyl group, one on the \(\mathrm{-OH}\)).

One mole of any substance contains \(6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\) particles, usually written \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\). This number is Avogadro's constant, \(N_A\), named in honour of Amedeo Avogadro (§1.8).

The particles counted are whatever entity the substance is made of — atoms, molecules or ions. The chapter's own examples make the point:

1 mole of oxygen atoms \(= 6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\) atoms of oxygen

1 mole of water molecules \(= 6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\) molecules of water

1 mole of sodium chloride \(= 6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\) formula units of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)

The count is the same in every case, which is why a mole is a counting unit rather than a mass.

The SI unit of the amount of a substance is the **mole**, whose symbol is **mol** (§1.8, and Table 1.1 of §1.3.1).

Two points the chapter is careful about. First, the name of the unit is *mole* and the symbol for the unit is *mol* — the two are not interchangeable in writing. Second, the amount of a substance is one of the seven SI BASE quantities, listed in Table 1.1 alongside length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature and luminous intensity, so the mole is a base unit and not a derived one.

The molar volume of a gas is the volume occupied by ONE MOLE of that gas at standard temperature and pressure. Chemists deduced from Avogadro's law that one mole of any gas occupies \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) at standard temperature (\(0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) and pressure (1 atm), and this volume of \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) is what is called the molar volume of a gas (§1.9).

The important feature is that it does not depend on which gas it is — it follows from Avogadro's law, since equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules. That is what makes it usable as a conversion factor:

\(\text{Number of moles of a gas } (n) = \dfrac{\text{Volume of the gas at STP}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}}\)

The chapter adds a note worth remembering: IUPAC has recently changed the standard pressure to 1 bar, and under those new STP conditions the molar volume is \(22.71\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\).

**Statement.** The law of conservation of mass states that 'mass can neither be created nor destroyed' (§1.4.1). Equivalently, in a chemical reaction

Total mass of reactants = Total mass of products

**Explanation.** The law came from Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794), the French chemist often called the father of modern chemistry. He carefully performed many combustion experiments — burning phosphorus and mercury, both in the presence of air — and both resulted in an increase in weight. After several experiments he found that the weight gained by the phosphorus was exactly the same as the weight lost by the air. Nothing had been created; mass had only moved from one substance to another.

The chapter's second illustration is the burning of hydrogen: when hydrogen gas burns and combines with oxygen to yield water, the mass of the water formed is equal to the combined mass of the hydrogen and the oxygen consumed.

Dalton's atomic theory explains why the law must hold: a chemical reaction involves only the reorganization of atoms, and atoms are neither created nor destroyed in it (§1.6). Since the same atoms are present before and after, the total mass cannot change.

The law of multiple proportions (§1.4.3), proposed by John Dalton in 1803, states:

When two elements A and B form more than one compound, the masses of element B that combine with a given mass of A are always in the ratio of small whole numbers.

The chapter's illustration: hydrogen and oxygen form both water and hydrogen peroxide. In water, 2 g of hydrogen combines with 16 g of oxygen; in hydrogen peroxide, the same 2 g of hydrogen combines with 32 g of oxygen. The two masses of oxygen taken by a fixed mass of hydrogen are therefore in the ratio 16 : 32, that is 1 : 2 — a ratio of small whole numbers.

Note the condition the law places on itself: it compares two compounds of the SAME pair of elements. Nitrogen and oxygen behave the same way in nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide (again 16 : 32, or 1 : 2), as do carbon and oxygen in \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).

A **solution**, such as common salt dissolved in water.

The chapter's own wording is that solutions are homogeneous mixtures, because the molecules of the constituent solute and solvent are uniformly mixed throughout its bulk (§1.2.2). That uniformity is the defining test: any sample drawn from anywhere in the salt solution has the same composition and the same properties as any other.

Sea water, listed in the chapter's opening 'Can you tell?', is another example.

A **suspension of an insoluble solid in a liquid** — the chapter's own example, such as chalk powder stirred into water (§1.2.2).

In a heterogeneous mixture the molecules of the constituents are NOT uniformly mixed throughout the bulk, so different samples taken from different parts of it can differ in composition. Concrete, listed earlier in the same section as a mixture of sand, cement and water, is another example: its constituents remain visibly separate.

**Gold (Au)**, one of the metals the chapter names.

An element is a pure substance which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical changes (§1.2.2). Elements are further classified as metals, non-metals and metalloids, and the chapter's examples are gold, silver, copper and iron (metals); iodine, nitrogen and carbon (non-metals); arsenic, silicon and germanium (metalloids). Any one of these is an acceptable answer.

**Water \((\mathrm{H_2O})\)**.

Compounds are the pure substances which CAN be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical changes, and in a compound two or three elements are combined in a fixed proportion (§1.2.2). Water qualifies on both counts: it is made of hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed proportion by mass (11.1 % and 88.9 %), and it can be decomposed into those two elements.

Sodium chloride \((\mathrm{NaCl})\) and mercuric oxide, both named in the chapter, are equally good answers.

One mole of ANY substance contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) particles of that substance (§1.8) — the count does not depend on what the substance is or on how heavy its molecules are.

Number of molecules in 1 mole of \(\mathrm{NH_3} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\)

Number of molecules in 1 mole of \(\mathrm{HNO_3} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\)

Ratio \(= \dfrac{6.022 \times 10^{23}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 1 : 1\)

The ratio is **1 : 1**. Note that the two are very different in MASS — the molar mass of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is \(17\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) and that of \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) is \(63\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) — but the question asks about the number of molecules, and equal numbers of moles always hold equal numbers of molecules.

First put the volume in the units the molar volume uses. The chapter gives \(1\ \mathrm{L} = 1\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) (§1.3.2 iii), so 0.448 litre is \(0.448\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).

Molar volume of a gas at STP \(= 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\) (§1.9)

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{\text{Volume of the gas at STP}}{\text{Molar volume of gas}}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.448\ \mathrm{dm^3}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}}\)

\(= 0.02\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The number of moles of hydrogen gas is **0.02 mol**. (Because the molar volume is the same for every gas, this answer would be unchanged for 0.448 litre of any other gas at STP.)

The mass of one atom of hydrogen is given as \(1.008\ \mathrm{u}\), so the mass of \(N\) such atoms is simply \(N\) times that.

Mass of 18 atoms of hydrogen

\(= 18 \times 1.008\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= 18.144\ \mathrm{u}\)

The mass is **18.144 u**. Keep the unit in u: the question gives the atomic mass on the unified-mass-unit scale and asks for the mass of a counted number of atoms, so no conversion to grams and no use of Avogadro's constant is needed. (Should the mass in grams be wanted, multiply by \(1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g\ u^{-1}}\), giving \(3.013 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{g}\).)

The two parts differ only in the UNIT on the 254, and that changes the scale of the answer by a factor of Avogadro's constant.

**a. 254 u of iodine.** The atomic mass 127 u is the mass of one iodine atom (§1.7.1), so

Number of atoms \(= \dfrac{254\ \mathrm{u}}{127\ \mathrm{u\ atom^{-1}}} = 2\) atoms

**b. 254 g of iodine.** Here 127 must be read as the molar mass, \(127\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), since the molar mass in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass in u (§1.8).

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{254\ \mathrm{g}}{127\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of atoms \(= 2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}} = 1.2044 \times 10^{24}\) atoms

So 254 u of iodine is **2 atoms** and 254 g of iodine is **\(1.2044 \times 10^{24}\) atoms** — the same number 254 giving answers that differ by \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) times, purely because of the unit.

Pencil 'lead' is graphite, an allotrope of carbon, so treat the writing as carbon with molar mass \(12\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

**a. Number of moles of carbon in 5 mg.**

\(5\ \mathrm{mg} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}\)

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}}{12\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}\)

\(= 4.17 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**b. Number of carbon atoms in 12 mg.**

\(12\ \mathrm{mg} = 12 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}\)

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{12 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}}{12\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of atoms \(= 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 6.022 \times 10^{20}\) atoms

So the 5 mg of writing is about \(4.17 \times 10^{-4}\) mol of carbon, and 12 mg of it contains \(6.022 \times 10^{20}\) carbon atoms. The second part is deliberately set at 12 mg, one thousandth of the molar mass, so the mole count comes out at exactly \(10^{-3}\) mol.

Find the molar mass of glucose, then scale the price from 250 g up to one mole.

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

\(= 6 \times 12.0 + 12 \times 1.0 + 6 \times 16.0\)

\(= 72 + 12 + 96 = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Cost per gram \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{Rs}\ 40}{250\ \mathrm{g}} = \mathrm{Rs}\ 0.16\ \mathrm{g^{-1}}\)

Cost per mole \(= 0.16\ \mathrm{Rs\ g^{-1}} \times 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= \mathrm{Rs}\ 28.8\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)

The cost of glucose is **Rs 28.80 per mole**. (Equivalently: 250 g is \(250/180 = 1.389\) mol, and \(40/1.389 = \mathrm{Rs}\ 28.8\) per mole.)

[Textbook misprint: the isotopic mass of \(^{10}\mathrm{B}\) is printed as 10.13; it should read 10.013, which is the accepted exact mass of that isotope. The printed answer 10.81 is CORRECT — but only for 10.013, which gives 10.8138. Taking the data exactly as printed gives 10.8367, i.e. 10.84. The companion datum 11.009 for \(^{11}\mathrm{B}\) is printed correctly, and the abundances sum to exactly 100 %, so the single dropped zero is the only defect. The solution below solves the question as printed and then shows the intended calculation.]

The average atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the atomic masses of its isotopes, taking their relative abundances into account (§1.7.2):

\(\text{Average atomic mass} = \dfrac{(\text{mass of } ^{10}\mathrm{B})(\%) + (\text{mass of } ^{11}\mathrm{B})(\%)}{100}\)

Substituting the values as printed in the question:

\(= \dfrac{(10.13)(19.60) + (11.009)(80.40)}{100}\)

\(= \dfrac{198.548 + 885.124}{100}\)

\(= \dfrac{1083.672}{100} = 10.84\ \mathrm{u}\)

So the data AS PRINTED give an average atomic mass of **10.84 u**.

The textbook's printed answer is 10.81, and the difference is not a rounding one — it comes from the isotopic mass of \(^{10}\mathrm{B}\). The accepted exact mass of that isotope is 10.013 u, not 10.13 u; with 10.013 the same calculation gives

\(\dfrac{(10.013)(19.60) + (11.009)(80.40)}{100} = 10.81\ \mathrm{u}\)

which is both the book's printed answer and the accepted average atomic mass of boron. Work with 10.013 u if you want the book's number; the working itself is identical either way.

As a check on the method, note that the answer must lie between 10.013 and 11.009 and much nearer the second, because \(^{11}\mathrm{B}\) makes up 80.40 % of the sample — and 10.81 does.

The chapter relates the two scales by \(^\circ\mathrm{F} = \dfrac{9}{5}(^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 32\) (§1.3.2 v).

**a. \(40\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)**

\(^\circ\mathrm{F} = \dfrac{9}{5}(40) + 32 = 72 + 32 = 104\)

so \(40\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 104\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\).

**b. \(30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)**

\(^\circ\mathrm{F} = \dfrac{9}{5}(30) + 32 = 54 + 32 = 86\)

so \(30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 86\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\).

Both answers are sensible against the chapter's own calibration points, which put \(0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) at \(32\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\) and \(100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) at \(212\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\): 40 and 30 lie between those, and 104 and 86 lie correspondingly between 32 and 212.

Acetic acid is \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), containing 2 C, 4 H and 2 O.

Molar mass \(= 2 \times 12.0 + 4 \times 1.0 + 2 \times 16.0 = 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{22\ \mathrm{g}}{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.3667\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of molecules = Number of moles \(\times\) Avogadro's constant

\(= 0.3667\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{molecules\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 2.208 \times 10^{23}\) molecules

So 22 g of acetic acid is **0.3667 mol**, containing about **\(2.21 \times 10^{23}\) molecules**. (Carrying the truncated value 0.3666 mol through the second step, as the textbook does, gives \(2.2076 \times 10^{23}\) molecules — the same answer to three significant figures.)

This is a direct application of the law of conservation of mass (§1.4.1), which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed, so

Total mass of reactants = Total mass of products

The reactants are carbon and oxygen; the only product is carbon dioxide.

mass of carbon + mass of oxygen = mass of carbon dioxide

\(24\ \mathrm{g} + \text{mass of oxygen} = 88\ \mathrm{g}\)

mass of oxygen \(= 88 - 24 = 64\ \mathrm{g}\)

So **64 g of oxygen** must have been used.

The figures are consistent with the formula of the product, which is a useful check: 24 g of carbon is 2 mol, 64 g of oxygen is 2 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and 88 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (molar mass \(44\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is 2 mol — exactly one \(\mathrm{O_2}\) per carbon atom, as \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) requires.

**a. 0.4 mole of nitrogen.** The question supplies the average atomic mass of nitrogen, so read this as 0.4 mole of nitrogen ATOMS.

Number of atoms = Number of moles \(\times\) Avogadro's constant

\(= 0.4\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 2.4088 \times 10^{23}\) atoms

(If 'nitrogen' were instead read as the diatomic gas \(\mathrm{N_2}\), 0.4 mole of MOLECULES would contain twice as many atoms, \(4.8176 \times 10^{23}\). The wording is genuinely open, but the atomic mass given with the question points to the atomic reading, which is also the one the textbook's answer uses.)

**b. 1.6 g of sulfur.** Here the mass must first be converted to moles, using \(32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) as the molar mass.

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{1.6\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of atoms \(= 0.05\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 3.011 \times 10^{22}\) atoms

The two experiments make the same oxide of the same metal by two different routes, so compare the mass of oxygen combining with a FIXED mass of metal in each.

**First experiment.** 2.0 g of metal gives 3.2 g of oxide, so the oxygen taken up is \(3.2 - 2.0 = 1.2\ \mathrm{g}\).

Oxygen per gram of metal \(= \dfrac{1.2}{2.0} = 0.600\)

**Second experiment.** 1.42 g of metal gives 2.27 g of oxide, so the oxygen taken up is \(2.27 - 1.42 = 0.85\ \mathrm{g}\).

Oxygen per gram of metal \(= \dfrac{0.85}{1.42} = 0.599\)

The two ratios are the same to the precision of the data (0.600 and 0.599). Equivalently, the percentage of metal in the oxide is \(2.0/3.2 = 62.5\ \%\) in the first sample and \(1.42/2.27 = 62.6\ \%\) in the second.

So the same compound, prepared by two different methods, contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. That is the **law of definite proportions** (§1.4.2), which states that a given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight, irrespective of its source. It is sometimes called the law of definite composition.

Note why this is NOT the law of multiple proportions: that law needs TWO DIFFERENT compounds of the same two elements, and asks for a small whole-number ratio between them. Here only one oxide is involved, and the ratio found is 1 : 1 rather than a ratio of different small whole numbers.

One molecule of acetaldehyde, \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), contains 2 C atoms, 4 H atoms and 1 O atom. So one MOLE of acetaldehyde contains 2 mol of carbon, 4 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of oxygen, and two moles contain twice each of those.

**a. Number of moles of carbon** \(= 2 \times 2 = 4\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**b. Number of moles of hydrogen** \(= 2 \times 4 = 8\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**c. Number of moles of oxygen** \(= 2 \times 1 = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**d. Number of molecules of acetaldehyde**

\(= 2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{molecules\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 1.2044 \times 10^{24}\) molecules, that is \(12.044 \times 10^{23}\) molecules

Count the hydrogens with care: the formula \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) has three on the methyl group and one on the aldehyde group, four in all.

Magnesium oxide is \(\mathrm{MgO}\), one atom of each element, so its formula mass is the sum of the two average atomic masses (§1.7.4):

Formula mass of \(\mathrm{MgO} = 24 + 16 = 40\ \mathrm{u}\)

and therefore its molar mass is \(40\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

**i. 80 g of MgO**

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{80\ \mathrm{g}}{40\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**ii. 10 g of MgO**

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{10\ \mathrm{g}}{40\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The answers are **2 mol** and **0.25 mol**. Note that magnesium oxide is an ionic solid with no discrete molecules, so 'formula mass' rather than 'molecular mass' is the correct term here, exactly as the chapter says for sodium chloride.

Rearranging the relation of §1.9, the volume of a gas at STP is the number of moles times the molar volume:

Volume at STP = Number of moles \(\times\ 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\)

**i. 5 moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)**

\(= 5\ \mathrm{mol} \times 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}} = 112\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

**ii. 0.5 mole of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)**

\(= 0.5\ \mathrm{mol} \times 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}} = 11.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

So the volumes are **112 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\)** and **11.2 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\)**. The molar mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is never needed: at STP the volume depends only on the number of moles, which is Avogadro's law at work.

Start from the volume of oxygen and work back to the mass of potassium chlorate that must decompose.

**Moles of oxygen liberated** (§1.9):

\(n(\mathrm{O_2}) = \dfrac{6.72\ \mathrm{dm^3}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.3\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Relate that to \(\mathrm{KClO_3}\).** Potassium chlorate decomposes on heating as

\(2\,\mathrm{KClO_3} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{KCl} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2}\)

so 3 mol of oxygen come from 2 mol of \(\mathrm{KClO_3}\). (This balanced equation is not developed in this chapter; it is the one piece of information the question assumes from outside it.)

\(n(\mathrm{KClO_3}) = 0.3\ \mathrm{mol} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Convert to mass**, using the molar mass given in the question:

mass \(= 0.2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 122.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 24.5\ \mathrm{g}\)

**24.5 g** of potassium chlorate is required. The 2 : 3 step is the one place to be careful — using a 1 : 1 ratio instead would give 36.75 g, half as much again.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the number of hydrogen atoms as \(2.24 \times 10^{23}\); it should be \(2.25 \times 10^{23}\). The book's own chain — \(4 \times 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) — yields \(2.2474 \times 10^{23}\), which rounds to 2.25 at three significant figures, and the exact value \(2.2482 \times 10^{23}\) rounds the same way. The key ROUNDS its other three values correctly (N 1.1237 to 1.124, C and O 0.56185 to 0.562) and truncates only this one, so the inconsistency is inside a single printed answer. The other three printed values are correct.]

Urea, \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\), contains 2 N, 4 H, 1 C and 1 O per molecule.

Molar mass \(= 2 \times 14 + 4 \times 1 + 12 + 16 = 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Number of moles of urea \(= \dfrac{5.6\ \mathrm{g}}{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Each element's atom count is its number per molecule times the moles of urea times Avogadro's constant.

**Hydrogen** (4 per molecule):

\(4 \times 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.25 \times 10^{23}\) atoms

**Nitrogen** (2 per molecule):

\(2 \times 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.124 \times 10^{23}\) atoms

**Carbon** (1 per molecule):

\(1 \times 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 0.562 \times 10^{23}\) atoms

**Oxygen** (1 per molecule): the same as carbon, \(0.562 \times 10^{23}\) atoms

The counts stand in the ratio 4 : 2 : 1 : 1, matching the formula — a quick way to check the arithmetic. (The textbook prints \(2.24 \times 10^{23}\) for hydrogen, which is the same figure truncated rather than rounded at the third significant digit.)

Sulfur burnt in excess oxygen gives sulfur dioxide, one molecule of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) per atom of sulfur:

\(\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SO_2}\)

Because the oxygen is in excess, all the sulfur is consumed and it is the sulfur that fixes the amount of product.

Number of moles of sulfur \(= \dfrac{16\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol}\)

From the 1 : 1 ratio, moles of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) formed \(= 0.5\ \mathrm{mol}\).

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{SO_2} = 32 + 2 \times 16 = 64\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

mass of \(\mathrm{SO_2} = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol} \times 64\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 32\ \mathrm{g}\)

**32 g** of sulfur dioxide is produced. Conservation of mass checks it: 16 g of sulfur plus the 16 g of oxygen that 0.5 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) weighs gives exactly 32 g of product.

The term is needed because most elements are not made of identical atoms. Many naturally occurring elements exist as a mixture of more than one isotope, and isotopes have different atomic masses (§1.7.2). A single number for 'the' atomic mass of such an element would therefore be false for every one of its atoms.

What is used instead is the weighted average of the atomic masses of the isotopes, taking their relative abundances into account — the **average atomic mass**. Carbon is the chapter's worked case: it occurs as \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\) (98.892 %), \(^{13}\mathrm{C}\) (1.108 %) and a trace of \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\), and

\((12\,\mathrm{u})\left(\dfrac{98.892}{100}\right) + (13.00335\,\mathrm{u})\left(\dfrac{1.108}{100}\right) + \ldots = 12.011\ \mathrm{u}\)

No single carbon atom weighs 12.011 u; the value describes a bulk sample, which is what a chemist actually weighs out.

Two consequences the chapter draws. The atomic masses printed in the periodic table are in fact these average atomic masses. And for practical purposes the average is rounded off to the nearest whole number when it differs from it only by a small fraction — carbon 12.0 u, nitrogen 14.0 u, oxygen 16.0 u, chlorine 35.5 u, bromine 79.9 u.

**Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, element or compound, expressed in grams** (§1.8). Its unit is \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

The useful property is a numerical one: the molar mass of any element in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that element in u, and the molar mass of any polyatomic substance in grams is numerically equal to its molecular mass or formula mass in u.

| Substance | Atomic / molecular / formula mass (u) | Molar mass (\(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) |
|---|---|---|
| H | 1.0 u | 1.0 |
| C | 12.0 u | 12.0 |
| O | 16.0 u | 16.0 |
| \(\mathrm{O_2}\) | 32.0 u | 32.0 |
| \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) | 18.0 u | 18.0 |
| \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) | 58.5 u | 58.5 |

The chapter shows the equality is not a coincidence but follows from the definitions, by building the molar mass of oxygen atoms out of Avogadro's constant and the mass of one atom:

\(6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}} \times 16\ \mathrm{u\ atom^{-1}} \times 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g\ u^{-1}} = 16.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Molar mass is what converts a mass on a balance into a number of moles, through \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass in g}}{\text{molar mass in g mol}^{-1}}\).

Even a small amount of any substance contains a very large number of atoms or molecules, so counting them individually is hopeless. The mole is the quantitative adjective chemists use to express that count, in the same way that 'dozen' expresses twelve and 'gross' expresses one hundred and forty-four (§1.8).

**Definition.** One mole is the amount of a substance that contains \(6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\) particles or entities — atoms, molecules or ions. The name of the unit is *mole* and its symbol is *mol*; it is the seventh SI base quantity, for the amount of a substance.

**Where the number comes from.** It is not arbitrary. It is fixed by carbon-12: the mass of one carbon-12 atom is \(1.992648 \times 10^{-23}\) g and the mass of one mole of carbon atoms is 12 g, so

\(\dfrac{12\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{1.992648 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{g\ atom^{-1}}} = 6.0221367 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atom\ mol^{-1}}\)

This number is Avogadro's constant, \(N_A\), named in honour of Amedeo Avogadro.

**Why it matters.** The count is the same for every substance, so the mole links three things a chemist can otherwise not compare — the mass weighed out, the volume of a gas measured, and the number of particles reacting:

\(n = \dfrac{\text{mass in g}}{\text{molar mass in g mol}^{-1}} = \dfrac{\text{volume of gas at STP}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}}\), and number of particles \(= n \times N_A\)

**Formula mass is the term used in place of molecular mass for a substance that does not exist as discrete molecules** (§1.7.4). It is the sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms in the substance's formula unit.

**Why a separate term is needed.** Some substances, such as sodium chloride, do not contain discrete molecules as their constituent units. In a sodium chloride crystal the cationic (sodium) and anionic (chloride) entities are arranged in a three-dimensional structure: one \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) ion is surrounded by six \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions, all at the same distance from it, and each chloride likewise by six sodium ions. There is no single particle that is 'a molecule of NaCl' to weigh, so \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is only a formula used to represent the compound, and what its mass describes is a formula unit.

**Example.** For sodium chloride (Problem 1.4 of the chapter):

Formula mass of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) = average atomic mass of Na + average atomic mass of Cl

\(= 23.0\ \mathrm{u} + 35.5\ \mathrm{u} = 58.5\ \mathrm{u}\)

A second example from the same worked problem, showing how a bracketed group is handled:

Formula mass of \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} = 63.5 + 2\,(14 + 3 \times 16) = 187.5\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Molar volume of a gas is the volume occupied by one mole of that gas at STP, namely \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)** (§1.9). Standard temperature and pressure here mean \(0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 1 atm.

**Why one number serves for every gas.** Chemists deduced the value from Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. One mole is the same number of molecules whatever the gas, so at a fixed temperature and pressure it must occupy the same volume whatever the gas — the identity and the molar mass of the gas do not enter.

**Why it is useful.** Volume is far easier to measure for a gas than mass, and the molar volume converts one into moles directly:

Number of moles of a gas \((n) = \dfrac{\text{Volume of the gas at STP}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}}\)

and then the number of molecules follows as \(n \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\).

One caution the chapter records: IUPAC has recently changed the standard pressure to 1 bar, and under those new STP conditions the molar volume of a gas is \(22.71\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) rather than 22.4.

On the basis of chemical composition, matter is classified into **pure substances** and **mixtures** (§1.2.1, §1.2.2).

**Pure substances** have a definite chemical composition and always have the same properties regardless of their origin. Examples: a pure metal, distilled water. They divide further into:

- **Elements** — pure substances which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical changes. They are classified in turn as **metals** (lustrous, conduct heat and electricity, ductile, malleable — gold, silver, copper, iron), **non-metals** (no lustre, poor conductors, brittle — iodine, nitrogen, carbon) and **metalloids**, whose properties lie between the two (arsenic, silicon, germanium).
- **Compounds** — pure substances which CAN be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical changes, in which two or three elements are combined in a fixed proportion.

**Mixtures** contain two or more substances in no fixed proportions and may be separated by physical methods; having no definite composition, they have no definite properties. Examples: paint (oils, pigment, additive), concrete (sand, cement, water). They divide into:

- **Homogeneous** mixtures, in which the constituent molecules are uniformly mixed throughout the bulk. Solutions are of this kind.
- **Heterogeneous** mixtures, in which they are not — for example a suspension of an insoluble solid in a liquid.

Note that this classification is by CHEMICAL COMPOSITION. Matter can also be classified by its physical state as solid, liquid or gas (§1.2.3), and that is a different axis: water is one and the same compound in all three states.
